maintainer_vibe: Educational and process-driven. Maintainers treat contributions as teaching moments, celebrating first-time contributors with emojis and congratulations, while expecting strict adherence to PR conventions, coding standards, and testing requirements. Reviews are collaborative and pedagogical, focusing on both technical correctness and learner experience.
pr_guidelines: PR titles must follow conventional commits format: <type>(<scope>): <description>, with description under 30 characters. Types include fix, feat, refactor, docs. Do not include issue numbers in the title.

The PR description checklist is mandatory and must be genuinely completed, not just ticked off. Maintainers deprioritize low-effort or low-quality PRs with a `deprioritize` label and may close them within 5-7 days if the contributor is unresponsive or shows non-responsiveness.

PRs must target the freeCodeCamp main branch from a fork, not be edited directly through GitHub's web interface. Do not @mention maintainers or reviewers in your PR - they are busy and it comes across as rude. Use the community forum or Discord for questions.

Two approvals are required from moderators or dev-team before merging. For curriculum PRs, leave an LGTM comment and merge once approved. For platform changes, comment LGTM and mention @freeCodeCamp/dev-team for final review before merging.
raw_summary: freeCodeCamp runs a high-volume repository (46k forks, 455k stars, 45,612 closed PRs) with a heavily volunteer-driven review process. Issue quality is generally strong: reporters include detailed reproduction steps, and maintainers respond with educational content referencing W3C standards, code of conduct guidelines, and curriculum philosophy. First-time contributors are explicitly celebrated with congratulatory messages and emojis. However, the repository struggles with low-effort AI-generated PRs flooding issues, which maintainers address through a `deprioritize` label and a 5-7 day grace period before closing rather than immediate rejection. The review culture is pedagogical above all: since this is a learning platform, reviewers focus on whether changes will confuse or help learners, not just technical correctness. Review templates guide maintainers to be specific about file changes, use suggestion blocks, and reference the Explore AST helper tool for curriculum test improvements. Maintainers never push directly to repositories, require CI checks to pass before merging, and use squash-and-merge to keep git history clean. Stale PRs are closed after 21 days of inactivity following a moderator request for changes, with a `status: waiting update` or `status: waiting review` label system to track state.
maintainer_persona: Curriculum-focused volunteers who are teachers first and engineers second. They maintain strict process discipline but greet new contributors with genuine enthusiasm. They iterate extensively with contributors on feedback and prefer to educate rather than dismiss, even for low-effort submissions. The community is large (volunteer-run, 501(c)(3) charity) so maintainers are protective of their limited time, which manifests as firm but fair process enforcement rather than personal hostility.
top_dos: Follow the conventional PR title format and fill out the PR template checklist completely before submitting. Include screenshots for UI changes and indicate local testing has been done.

Engage with review feedback actively. Maintainers label PRs with `status: waiting update` when changes are requested and appreciate prompt, thorough iteration. The review on PR #69589 shows maintainers giving specific technical feedback (e.g., use AST helper, spyOn pattern) and contributors responding with targeted commits.
Test changes locally and reference the contributing guidelines. For behavioral or UI changes, include Playwright integration tests if applicable.
top_donts: Do not edit files directly through GitHub's web editor. All changes should come from a fork on a dedicated feature branch, tested locally or in Codespaces.

Do not @mention maintainers or reviewers in your PR description or comments. This is considered rude and maintainers are already monitoring incoming PRs in order. Use the freeCodeCamp Community forum or Discord for questions instead.

Do not submit low-effort PRs or AI-generated content without genuine engagement with the contribution guidelines. These get deprioritized with a `deprioritize` label and may be closed within 5-7 days without extensive discussion.

deep_sections.title: What Contributors Actually Say
deep_sections.body: Contributors praise the welcoming nature of the community in forum discussions. One first-time contributor described their experience: the reviewer was 'the one reviewing your PR' and engaged with specific line-by-line feedback, explaining why a suggested change was out of scope for the current PR and directing the contributor to open a separate issue instead. A DEV Community writer reflected that every PR is valuable and that following the Code of Conduct and contributing guides 'creates a lot more work for the maintainers in the end' when skipped. On the freeCodeCamp Forum, contributors recommend asking questions in the `#freecodecamp-community` channel or the freeCodeCamp Community forum category, not by pinging maintainers. The tone from both reviewers and contributors is consistently educational: reviewers teach through inline comments, and contributors report learning about the codebase through the review process itself.

deep_sections.title: Hidden Friction Signals
deep_sections.body: The repository employs a `deprioritize` label for low-quality or low-effort PRs, which signals to the dev-team that such PRs require less immediate attention. This label was applied specifically in response to contributor concerns about AI-generated code flooding issues, but the maintainers clarified it applies regardless of whether AI was used. PRs labeled `first timers only` that are submitted by existing contributors (not first-time) are closed to preserve the opportunity for newcomers. The FAQ states: 'We typically accept the most quality contribution followed by the one that is made first,' which means a later, higher-quality PR can supersede an earlier submission. Stale PRs are closed after 21 days of inactivity, but only after a moderator has requested changes and labeled the PR `status: waiting update`. The `status: waiting review` label is used when PRs are ready for QA but pending additional review. These labels function as a triage system that contributors rarely mention in documentation but which deeply affect review timing.

deep_sections.title: Unwritten Rules
deep_sections.body: Beyond the written contributing guide, several cultural norms govern successful contributions. Maintainers expect contributors to demonstrate genuine engagement with the codebase rather than surface-level fixes; the contributing FAQ explicitly states that not following the guidelines 'earns you the respect of fellow maintainers and saves everyone time.' The community does not assign issues - contributors simply open PRs against `help wanted` or `first timers only` issues, and the first quality PR is accepted. For curriculum changes, maintainers prioritize learner experience over technical purity: a review on PR #69589 rejected a spyOn-based test change because 'The test changes on step 27 are a bit strict and will probably throw a user off,' even though the new tests were technically correct. The use of `LGTM` (Looks Good To Me) and squash-and-merge is the standard approval and merge workflow. All code must enter through PRs from forks - moderators never push directly. The community also maintains a separate `@freecodecamp/ui` design system package, and contributors working on frontend components must reference the design style guide for colors, fonts, and accessibility standards. Playwright tests are expected for behavioral changes. Maintainers use the Explore AST helper tool for curriculum test improvements, and reviewers expect contributors to follow this established pattern rather than introducing new testing approaches.
